title: Lecture 15 – Retina
html:
Source: c15 retina.pptx – 33 slides

Retina #1

Retinal changes in systemic arterial hypertension #2

  • Signs and symptoms
  • parallel with systemic changes of arterial hypertension
  • four progressive stages of retinal involvement and its vessels

Retinal changes in systemic arterial hypertension #3

  • Signs and symptoms
  • Retinal angiopathy
  • mild narrowing the arterial caliber
  • dilations and tortuosity of the retinal veins;
  • variations of tension within the central retinal artery

Retinal changes in systemic arterial hypertension #4

  • Signs and symptoms
  • Retinal angiosclerozis
  • arteries appear with a longitudinal central reflex
  • sclerosis of the vascular wall,
  • russet and wide (copper wirings)
  • white greyish and narrow (silver wirings)
  • Salus Gunn sign
  • changes at the arteriovenous crossings
  • structural shrinkage of arterial size with nipping and obstruction of the retinal vein behind the crossing;
  • pressure within central retinal artery is augmented,

Retinal changes in systemic arterial hypertension #5

  • Signs and symptoms
  • Hypertensive retinopathy
  • signs outlined above
  • dot and blot hemorrhages
  • scattered flame-shaped hemorrhages
  • in the nerve fiber layer of the retina
  • soft and hard exudates peripapillary and perimacular;
  • hard exudates
  • may radiate from the macula causing a star figure to emerge.
  • soft exudates (cotton wool spots)
  • focal ischemic changes due to localized closure of the retinal capillaries
  • evidence of the severity of the condition

Retinal changes in systemic arterial hypertension #6

  • Signs and symptoms
  • Hypertensive retinopathy
  • hemorrhages and exudates are usually symptomless
  • Except
  • vitreous hemorrhage
  • the deposits involve the macula.
  • visual symptoms
  • accelerated or malignant hypertension
  • longstanding disease,
  • flashes of light
  • intermittent loss of vision
  • spasm of the arteries
  • Depress of vision
  • significant macular edema

Retinal changes in systemic arterial hypertension #7

  • Signs and symptoms
  • Hypertensive neuroretinopathy
  • signs mentioned above,
  • edema of the optic disk
  • sometimes associated with edema of the macula

Retinal changes in systemic arterial hypertension #8

  • Treatment
  • reducing the blood pressure to as normal
  • cardiovascular specialist

Retinal changes in diabetes #9

  • Diabetic retinopathy
  • the most important ocular complication of diabetes.
  • mostly 8-10 years after the beginning of the diabetes in patients over 50 years of age (maturity-onset diabetes)
  • sometimes it may be the first sign of the diabetes
  • about 50% of diabetic patients develop retinopathy.

Retinal changes in diabetes #10

  • Pathogenesis
  • microaneurysms (capillary dilations)
  • retinal capillaries lose their pericytes causing the vascular wall resistance to lower
  • capillary tears determine retinal hemorrhages
  • retinal exudates and retinal edema
  • by leakage from the capillary wall,
  • obstruction of retinal capillaries
  • retinal ischemia
  • retinal angiogenesal factor (VEGF)
  • retinal neovascularization aiming at nutrition of hypoxic retina.

Retinal changes in diabetes #11

  • Signs and symptoms.
  • Nonproliferative background diabetic retinopathy
  • lesions usually temporally from the macula
  • (1) microaneurysms;
  • (2) blot hemorrhages within or upon the retina;
  • (3) lipidic hard exudates;
  • (4) retinal edema
  • (5) venous dilations.
  • little effect on the vision
  • unless the macula is affected
  • if macular edema is present can seriously impair the vision.

Preproliferative diabetic retinopathy #12

  • (1) intraretinal microvascular anomalies (vascular bypasses);
  • (2) ischemic retinal infarcts with cotton wool spots or soft white-greysh exudates;
  • extensive areas where capillary bed is closed (capillary nonperfusion zones) leading to retinal anoxia and hypoxia;
  • (3) severe macular edema.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (retinitis proliferans) #13

  • neovascularization
  • new vessel formation on the retina or optic disk
  • prone to leakage
  • bleeding repeatedly into the vitreous.
  • preretinal and vitreous hemorrhages
  • eventually associated with fibro-glial proliferation infiltrating the vitreous structure.
  • irregular shrinkage pulls away the retina resulting in traction retinal detachment.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (retinitis proliferans) #14

  • sight strongly depressed
  • the angiogenesal factor (VEGF) produced by hypoxic retina may pass into the anterior segment
  • rubeosis iridis and neovascular glaucoma

Treatment #15

  • background diabetic retinopathy without maculopathy
  • patient ophthalmologically assessed every 6 months
  • preproliferative diabetic retinopathy
  • laser retinal photocoagulation.
  • the laser is directed towards the hypoxic areas of the retina
  • the associated microaneurysms are also destroyed and cannot therefore bleed anymore.

Treatment #16

  • proliferative diabetic retinopathy
  • panretinal photocoagulation
  • destroying the peripheral retina
  • exception of the central retinal zone.
  • the principle of converting hypoxic areas of capillary closure to anoxic scars by photocoagulation
  • widely applied in proliferative diabetic retinopathy,
  • particularly when neovascularization of the optic disk is well developed.
  • antiangiogenezal agents
  • bevacizumab, ranibizumab, aflibercept
  • vitrectomy
  • advanced proliferative retinopathy.

Retinitis pigmentosa pigmentary retinopathy #17

  • the condition appears in childhood
  • hereditarily transmitted;
  • sex-linked recessive mode is common.
  • Symptoms
  • hesperanopya = poor night vision or even night blindness
  • sees well during the daylight
  • difficulties in in the evening and during the night
  • visual field concentrically restrained;
  • tunnel vision

Retinitis pigmentosa #18

  • Signs
  • retinal arteries are attenuated,
  • papilla is yellow
  • waxy pale aspect
  • dendritic black pigmented cells
  • bone corpuscle shaped clumps of pigment in the mid periphery of the retina.
  • absence of the electroretinogramm
  • earliest signs.

Retinitis pigmentosa #19

  • Pathogenesis
  • a progressive degeneration of the sensory retina
  • the rod cells that first affected,
  • the cones later
  • Atrophic retina
  • secondary migration of the pigment from the retinal pigment epithelium within the other retinal layers.
  • Treatment
  • pituitary extract topically given as a pigment controller trying to arrest the evolution of the disease.

Retinal detachment #20

  • separation of the retinal pigment epithelium that remains adherent to Bruch’s membrane from the other remainder retinal layers
  • serosity, exudation, hemorrhage ,tumor
  • separates the rods and cones from the contact with their source of nutrition, leaving them functionless even if they do no die

Secondary #21

  • conditions :
  • Trauma
  • penetrating injuries
  • severe blunt injuries (concussions)
  • choroidal inflammation
  • choroidal tumors
  • (uveal malignant melanoma, secondary deposits from breast carcinoma, etc)
  • advanced diabetic retinopathy
  • traction detachment associated with organized vitreous hemorrhage

Primary rhegmatogenous retinal detachment #22

  • Etiopathogenesis
  • retinal tear or hole ;
  • the liquefied vitreous enters the retina producing separation
  • after a small traumatism by predisposed patients:
  • high myopes with large eyes and stretched retinae;
  • mechanical tears or holes of the inner retinal layers ;
  • elderly patients with arteriosclerosis
  • have peripheral degenerations of the retina

Symptoms #23

  • visual field defect
  • shadow corresponding to the detached area
  • the detachment extends so that the shadow becomes gradually larger
  • eventually the macula is stripped off,
  • the central vision is lost
  • flying flies, distorted vision,
  • flashes of light or electric sparks,
  • symptomatic for retinal hole formation although the process of hole formation may be symptomless
  • vitreous hemorrhage coming from the torn retina
  • metamorphopsia
  • straight line appearing to have a kink,

Signs #24

  • the retina presents a yellow-greyish and wrinkled prominance that may undulate as the eye moves
  • one or more retinal tears of the internal layers of the retina localized in the detached area of the retina
  • usually in the supero-temporal quadrant
  • retinal vessels appear narrow, tortuous and wrinkled;
  • they have a dark color because are no longer in close contact with the red glow given by the choroidal vascular background,
  • responsabile for the normal red reflex seen with the ophthalmoscope

Retinoblastoma #25

  • Signs
  • first stage
  • a retinal detachment
  • second stage
  • leukocoria (white yellowish colour in the pupil)
  • third stage,
  • secondary glaucoma
  • growing the tumoral mass
  • embarrassement aqueous humor circulation
  • within the eye
  • outflow from the eyeball
  • last stage
  • dissemination within the orbit, bones and central nervous system

Diagnostic considerations and findings: #26

  • Central retinal vein occlusion
  • linear or punctiform hemorrhages in all four quadrants of the retina
  • distended and increasingly meandering veins.
  • branch retinal vein occlusion,
  • intraretinal hemorrhages in the area of vascular supply;
  • one quadrant or in two quadrants (hemispheric vein occlusion).

Diagnostic considerations and findings: #27

  • Cotton-wool spots and retinal or optic-disk edema
  • non-ischemic and ischemic occlusion
  • depending on the extent of capillary occlusion
  • diagnosed with fluorescein angiography
  • Complications
  • preretinal neovascularization,
  • retinal detachment,
  • Neovascular glaucoma.
  • Treatment:`
  • Anti VEGF
  • Laser photocoagulation in ichemic condition

Retinal Arterial Occlusion #28

  • Retinal infarction due to occlusion of an artery in the lamina cribrosa or a branch retinal artery occlusion.
  • Etiology:
  • Emboli
  • Inflammatory processes
  • temporal arteritis
  • Symptoms:
  • In central retinal artery occlusion,
  • sudden, painless unilateral blindness.
  • branch retinal artery occlusion,
  • loss of visual acuity or visual field defects.

Diagnostic considerations: #29

  • Acute stage
  • retina grayish white
  • edema of the layer of optic nerve fibers and
  • no longer transparent.
  • cherry red spot
  • the fovea centralis, (no nerve fibers),
  • the red of the choroid
  • The column of blood interrupted.
  • Rarely embolus.
  • chronic stage
  • Atrophy of the optic

Branch retinal artery occlusion, #30

  • retinal edema in the affected area of vascular supply
  • Perimetry
  • total visual field defect in central retinal artery occlusion
  • partial defect in branch occlusion.

Patients with a cilioretinal artery #31

  • artery originating from the ciliary arteries
  • normal perfusion in the area of vascular supply,
  • less loss of visual acuity
  • Treatment:
  • unsuccessful
  • Ocular massage, medications to reduce IOP,
  • an attempt to drain the embolus in a peripheral retinal vessel.
  • Calcium antagonists or hemodilution are in an attempt to improve vascular supply.
  • Lysis therapy
  • poor prognosis (it is not able to prevent blindness)
  • the risk to vital tissue involved.

Retinoblastoma #32

  • Treatment
  • large tumors,
  • enucleation
  • small and middle size tumors
  • radiotherapy with episcleral plaque of iodine or cobalt
  • an alternative to enucleation
  • should perforate the eyeball
  • exenteration of the orbit

Retinal Vein Occlusion #33

  • The most frequent underlying disorders
  • systemic
  • arterial hypertension and diabetes mellitus;
  • ocular disorder
  • Glaucoma
  • Etiology:
  • local thrombosis at sites where sclerotic arteries compress the veins
  • central retinal vein occlusion, lamina cribrosa;
  • branch retinal vein occlusion, arteriovenous crossing.
  • Symptoms:
  • loss of visual acuity if the macula or optic disk are involved.
